analysis.evidence: וַאֲנִי singles out God as the speaker. The following הִנְנִי מֵבִיא, “I am about to bring,” resumes the first person and identifies bringing the flood as God's own action.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וַ־ prefixed to an independent first-person common singular pronoun.
analysis.sense: I, as for me (the speaker set apart)

analysis.evidence: The suffix in הִנְנִי refers back to the emphatic וַאֲנִי (“as for me”). The following participle מֵבִיא (“bringing”) identifies the action God announces: he is about to bring the flood upon the earth.
analysis.morphology: Presentative particle with a first-person common singular pronominal suffix.
analysis.sense: look, I am about to (announcing an act)

analysis.evidence: הִנְנִי with מֵבִיא presents the speaker’s action as impending. אֶת marks הַמַּבּוּל as what he will bring, and עַל הָאָרֶץ identifies where the flood will come.
analysis.morphology: Hiphil active participle, masculine singular absolute
analysis.sense: bring someone or something to a destination

analysis.evidence: In מֵבִיא אֶת הַמַּבּוּל, אֶת marks הַמַּבּוּל (“the flood”) as the definite direct object of מֵבִיא (“bringing”).
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle without prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add Genesis 1:6 to the existing physical body-of-water sense in mayim.
draft.definition: A body or flow of water, including the waters on either side of the expanse.
draft.evidence: Genesis 1:6 repeats מַיִם on either side of the expression of separation. The expanse divides the waters already mentioned in the verse.

analysis.evidence: In הַמַּבּוּל מַיִם, מַיִם identifies the waters of the flood that God says he will bring upon the earth.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural common noun in the absolute state, without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: a body or flow of water

analysis.evidence: In עַל הָאָרֶץ, עַל marks where God says he will bring the floodwaters: upon the earth.
In עַל הָאָרֶץ, the earth is where the floodwaters will come. The phrase מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמָיִם (“under the heavens”) frames the flood’s reach as the whole earth.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הָ־ + common noun, singular absolute, of common gender.

analysis.evidence: לְשַׁחֵת states the purpose of bringing the flood. Its object is כָּל־בָּשָׂר, “all flesh,” and the closing verb יִגְוָע, “will perish,” confirms that destruction here means loss of life.
analysis.morphology: Piel infinitive construct with prefixed לְ expressing purpose

analysis.evidence: In לְשַׁחֵת כָּל בָּשָׂר, “to destroy all flesh,” כָּל quantifies the collective noun בָּשָׂר. The clause אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ רוּחַ חַיִּים identifies the group in view as all flesh that has the breath of life.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular noun in the construct state, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In כָּל בָּשָׂר, “all flesh,” the clause אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ רוּחַ חַיִּים identifies the creatures in view as those with the breath of life. The closing words כֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ יִגְוָע, “everything on earth will perish,” confirm the collective sense.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine singular absolute, used collectively.
analysis.sense: all flesh: every living creature; mankind

analysis.evidence: אֲשֶׁר introduces a relative clause modifying כָּל בָּשָׂר (“all flesh”). The suffix in בּוֹ (“in it”) refers back to בָּשָׂר, giving the reading “all flesh in which there is the breath of life.”
רוּחַ forms a construct phrase with חַיִּים, “breath of life.” The clause אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ רוּחַ חַיִּים describes all flesh that has this breath within it and will perish in the flood.
analysis.morphology: Common-gender noun, singular construct, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In רוּחַ חַיִּים, “breath of life,” חַיִּים supplies the “of life” part of the phrase. The verse identifies the flesh that will perish in the flood as flesh that has this breath within it.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural absolute noun, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: life as given by God's breath

analysis.evidence: מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמָיִם means “from beneath the heavens.” The phrase identifies the place from which the flood will destroy all flesh that has the breath of life.
analysis.morphology: Preposition תַּחַת with prefixed מִן. The נ assimilates to the initial ת, marked by dagesh.

analysis.evidence: מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמָיִם means “beneath the sky.” The closing clause כֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ יִגְוָע identifies those beneath the sky as the living creatures on earth that will perish.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ prefixed to a masculine plural noun in the absolute state.

analysis.evidence: כֹּל stands on its own as the subject of יִגְוָע ‘will perish’. The relative clause אֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ ‘that is on the earth’ restricts its scope to the living things described earlier in the verse.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute noun, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In כֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ יִגְוָע, ‘everything that is on the earth will perish,’ אֲשֶׁר introduces the relative clause בָּאָרֶץ, which modifies כֹּל.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected relative particle without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In כֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ יִגְוָע, בָּאָרֶץ locates everything that will perish. The preceding מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמָיִם, “under the heavens,” identifies the earth as the realm in view.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, singular absolute, common gender, with prefixed בְּ and the definite article.

draft.change: Add a root article for גוע with the Qal sense ‘to die’.
draft.definition: To die, of a person or an animal.
draft.evidence: Genesis 6:17 predicts that the creatures with the breath of life will perish. Genesis 7:21–22 recounts the fulfillment, using גוע and then מוּת of those who died.

analysis.evidence: The flood will destroy all flesh that has the breath of life. The closing clause כֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ יִגְוָע states what will happen to those creatures: everything on earth will perish.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, third person masculine singular, with preformative יִ־ and no suffix. The singular agrees with כֹּל.
